description: Car Hacking Village focuses on vehicle security research, CAN bus injection attacks, EV charging side channels, automotive USB kernel fuzzing, and cryptographic validation.

talks.title: Exploiting Wireless Side Channels in EV Charging
talks.teaser: Demonstrates wireless electromagnetic leakage in EV Combined Charging System (CCS) cables, using SDRs to eavesdrop on power-line communications and disrupt charging.
talks.summary:
Electromagnetic Leakage in EV Charging Cables

The Combined Charging System (CCS) and North American Charging Standard (NACS) utilize Power-Line Communication (PLC) over physical charging cables for vehicle-to-charger telemetry.

Eavesdropping via Unintentional Radiated Emissions

Sebastian Köhler and Richard Baker demonstrate that unshielded charging cables act as broadcast antennas, radiating high-frequency HomePlug Green PHY PLC signals into ambient space.

Wireless Injection and Denial-of-Service with SDRs

Using low-cost software-defined radios (SDRs), an attacker within hundreds of meters can passively intercept session tokens or inject malicious frames to terminate EV charging cycles abruptly.

Standardization Shortcomings and Hardware Hardening

The authors analyze why architectural flaws persist across global EV standards and outline hardware shielding and cryptographic countermeasures for charging networks.

talks.title: How an Auto Security Researcher Had His Car Stolen
talks.teaser: Automotive security experts reverse engineer a real-world CAN Injection theft tool disguised as a Bluetooth speaker used to steal a Toyota RAV4.
talks.summary:
Investigating the Theft of a 2021 Toyota RAV4

When automotive security researcher Ian Tabor's vehicle was stolen from his driveway, he tracked down physical forensic evidence pointing to an emerging attack method known as CAN Injection.

Reverse Engineering the Hardware Theft Tool

Ian Tabor and Ken Tindell acquire and dissect the criminal hardware device—cleverly concealed inside a modified JBL Bluetooth speaker enclosure.

Exploiting Headlight Wiring to Inject CAN Frames

By accessing the vehicle's CAN bus wiring behind the front bumper headlight assembly, the rogue device silences legitimate Electronic Control Units (ECUs) and injects forged door-unlock and immobilizer-disable commands.

Industry Remediation and Cryptographic Message Authentication

The authors detail their coordinated vulnerability disclosure with Toyota, urging automakers to adopt cryptographic CAN message authentication (SecOC) to thwart physical bus injection.

talks.title: Automotive USB Fuzzing
talks.teaser: Presents an in-vehicle USB kernel fuzzing framework directly connected to production vehicles, discovering zero-days across Volkswagen, Renault, GM, and AGL.
talks.summary:
The Limitations of Conventional Automotive Media Fuzzing

Automotive security evaluations typically test In-Vehicle Infotainment (IVI) media decoders in isolated desktop emulators rather than testing live hardware connected to in-vehicle buses.

Developing Direct In-Vehicle USB Fuzzing Frameworks

Euntae Jang, Donghyon Jeong, and Jonghyuk Song introduce an automated USB fuzzing harness that connects directly to production vehicle head units over physical USB interfaces.

Fuzzing Automotive Kernel Drivers and Media Parsers

Injecting malformed USB descriptor packets and corrupt media streams uncovered severe memory corruption flaws in operating system kernels and Automotive Grade Linux (AGL) distributions.

Real-World Zero-Days Across Major Automakers

Case studies detail reproducible crash and code execution vulnerabilities identified in production Volkswagen Jetta, Renault Zoe, and Chevrolet Equinox infotainment systems.

talks.title: Abusing CAN Bus Spec for DoS in Embedded Systems
talks.teaser: Martin Petran explores exploiting edge cases in the CAN bus protocol specification and message metadata fields to induce denial-of-service across embedded ECUs.
talks.summary:
The Absolute Truth of Protocol Specifications

Controller Area Network (CAN) bus implementations strictly adhere to formal ISO standards, leading embedded firmware developers to make dangerous assumptions about message formats.

Violating Specification Assumptions in CAN Frames

Martin Petran evaluates what occurs when an adversary crafts non-compliant CAN messages, manipulating reserved metadata bits and unexpected payload lengths.

Triggering Denial-of-Service in Commercial Driver Stacks

Auditing proprietary and open-source CAN transceivers and microcontroller driver libraries revealed unhandled exceptions and buffer state desynchronizations that freeze embedded controllers.

Defensive Verification for Automotive Software

The author provides test suites and defensive software patterns for embedded developers to validate raw CAN frames safely without relying on hardware-level assumptions.

talks.title: A SSLippery Slope: Unraveling Hidden Dangers of Certificate Misuse
talks.teaser: Bill Demirkapi uncovers systemic validation flaws in digital signature implementations, allowing attackers to repurpose incompatible certificates to sign untrusted code.
talks.summary:
The Critical Role of Code Signing Certificates

Digital code signing certificates undergo rigorous identity vetting to establish publisher trust, ensuring operating systems only execute authenticated binaries and firmware updates.

Discovering Systemic Signature Validation Flaws

Bill Demirkapi investigates parsing logic across major operating system loaders and signature verification APIs, discovering critical oversights in Enhanced Key Usage (EKU) checks.

Bypassing Trust Boundaries with Incompatible Certificates

Vulnerable verifiers mistakenly accept signatures generated by cheap or unrelated TLS/S-MIME certificates as valid code signing credentials, allowing adversaries to sign malicious payloads.

Hardening Cryptographic Verification Pipelines

The author outlines comprehensive remediation steps for operating system developers and software vendors to strictly enforce certificate purpose constraints and signature chain validation.

talks.title: VDA Shenanigans: Attacking & Defending the Truck Part that Gets Left Behind
talks.teaser: Wyatt Ford and Alex Reuter investigate security weaknesses in Vehicle Diagnostic Adapters (VDAs) used on heavy commercial trucks, exploring firmware updates and attack surfaces.
talks.summary:
Insecure Firmware Updates in Heavy Vehicle Adapters

Vehicle Diagnostic Adapters (VDAs) connect commercial truck electronics to diagnostic computers, playing a vital role in maintenance and heavy-duty fleet operations. Despite their privileged access to vehicle control units and diagnostic networks, VDAs frequently suffer from lax firmware update validation.

Attacking the Overlooked Interface

Wyatt Ford and Alex Reuter reverse engineer standard commercial VDAs to expose common software vulnerabilities and unprotected communication interfaces. They demonstrate how an attacker can leverage vulnerable adapter hardware to bridge external networks directly onto the truck's J1939 and CAN buses.

Defensive Architecture and Telematics Hardening

The speakers propose concrete architectural improvements for fleet operators and hardware manufacturers, emphasizing cryptographic signature verification on adapter firmware, secure boot enforcement, and rigorous physical interface auditing.
